chunks.text: Learning through the Cryo-EM Forward Model Figure 2: Augmentations can be unphysical . (A) 2D rotations of an image do not span all possible rotations of a 3D protein. (B) Image-space crops and blurs do not translate to the cryo-EM forward model. Many self-supervised learning methods use multiple views of the same observation as a training signal, using augmentations that alter image appearance while preserving semantic content. When explicitly rendering new observations is impractical, as in natural scenes, image-space augmentations such as crops, rotations, color perturbations, and blur provide useful proxies for variation in the imaging process. For example, a 2D rotation corresponds to an in-plane camera rotation, while Gaussian blur can approximate optical or motion blur. The same strategy, however, is less natural for cryo-EM. Transformations of an already projected particle image do not, in general, correspond to varying the latent variables of the cryo-EM forward model while holding structure fixed. For example, rotating a particle image, as in Cryo-IEF, changes only its in-plane orientation and cannot generate a different out-of-plane projection (Figure 2 ). Similarly, Gaussian blur does not reproduce a change in defocus, whose effect is governed by the oscillatory contrast transfer function. Thus, generic image-space augmentations may induce invariances that do not correspond to physically realizable variation in cryo-EM. However, high-fidelity explicit forward models for cryo-EM already exist, such as CryoJAX ( O’Brien et al., 2026 ) . Instead of approximating changes to the image formation process with 2D augmentations, we can directly render alternate observations of the same structure: y i ∼ p ⁡ ( y ∣ X k , R i , C i , t i , … ) y_{i}\sim p(y\mid X_{k},R_{i},C_{i},t_{i},\ldots) (2) while varying the latent quantities that determine how a fixed molecular structure is observed.

We engineered CryoJAX to render these views fast enough to run inside the training loop. This lets us train models with SSL with grounded positive pairs without the cost generally associated with rendering. Given this, the remaining question is which SSL objective should learn from these pairs. Contrastive objectives additionally require defining negative examples, which is difficult in cryo-EM. Two different particle images can arise from the same molecular structure, while their visual similarity or dissimilarity may instead be a function of their pose or imaging conditions. We use DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) for image-level self-distillation and complement it with the iBOT masked-patch objective ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) to supervise spatially resolved features without needing explicit negative pairs. Probing Structural Information in Experimental Images We first test if the representations learned by EMber can organize experimental particles consistently enough to recover dataset identity without learning task-specific readouts. Following prior work, we build a k k -nearest neighbor classifier over 29 experimental particle datasets from CryoPPP ( Dhakal et al., 2023 ) . As shown in Table 5 , models are able to easily discriminate between EMPIAR datasets in latent space. EMber ViT-S reaches 92.17% Top-1 accuracy and 99.77% Top-5 accuracy, with larger models saturating quickly. At comparable model sizes, EMber improves over Cryo-IEF and CryoUNI. Particle images from apo (EMPIAR-10005) and ligand-bound (EMPIAR-10059) TRPV1 datasets occupy overlapping regions in dimensionality reduction plots (Appendix Fig. 11 ), consistent with their shared molecular identity. However, this result is difficult to interpret biologically. EMPIAR datasets vary the molecule being imaged and acquisition-specific factors. This experiment shows that the representation captures strong and reproducible signal in experimental particles, but not which part of that signal is structural.

Next, we design a more controlled experimental setting to isolate molecular composition from imaging conditions. Compositional discrimination under controlled imaging conditions. Figure 3: Compositional heterogeneity classification on CAHRA experimental data. (A) Fine-tuning accuracy versus model FLOPs, with a supervised ResNet-18 reference. (B) Accuracy versus model FLOPs when linear probing frozen backbones, with a reference supervised ResNet-18. (C) Pooled linear/MLP readouts with a convolutional head that preserves spatial information. To directly test whether frozen representations retain molecular information, we use the CAHRA compositional heterogeneity challenge ( Feathers et al., 2026 ) which contains labeled particles from six proteins collected under similar microscopy conditions which are not seen during pre-training. We fine-tune the pre-trained backbones for this task, as well as multiple probes on frozen features. On pooled features, we train linear and MLP probes, and on the unpooled two-dimensional patch features we train a convolutional probe. Full details are in Appendix C . The results when fine-tuning the encoders is shown in Fig. 3 A. Across all model sizes EMber is the only model which outperforms the fully-supervised baseline ResNet-18. Fig. 3 B shows that compositional information is already linearly accessible from frozen representations. EMber -g reaches 79.76% with a linear probe, only 2.65 percentage points below the fully supervised ResNet-18, and outperforms Cryo-IEF and CryoUNI at comparable model sizes. Fig. 3 C tests whether pooling discards useful information. Across all pre-trained backbones, the parameter-matched convolutional probe outperforms the MLP. EMber -B reaches 82.72%, comparable to the supervised baseline. As the trend is similar for Cryo-IEF and CryoUNI, this result supports retaining the spatial organization of patch features rather than attributing the gain solely to our patch-level objective.

Conclusion We introduce EMber , a family of general cryo-EM representations learned with self-supervision through the cryo-EM forward model. Our evaluations provide a framework for studying what cryo-EM representations retain: distinguishing dataset discrimination from evidence of molecular information, comparing global and spatial readouts, and testing whether those representations support downstream structural inference. Across frozen probing, fine-tuning, population estimation, and reconstruction, EMber sets a new performance-compute frontier across several structural inference problems, while our analyses show that biologically relevant information is retained in both global and spatial features. Our results provide a practical recipe for scaling representation learning on cryo-EM data: use the forward model to construct physically meaningful supervision, combine structurally precise simulated data with diverse experimental particles, and reuse the resulting representation across downstream analyses. There remains substantial room to improve how simulated and experimental data are mixed, how spatial features are supervised under extreme noise, and how much experimental diversity can be recovered from currently deposited particle data. Nevertheless, the breadth of transfer we observe suggests that representation learning on noisy cryo-images alone can learn to solve multiple inverse problems without explicit supervision, and opens the door to extending the same approach to micrographs, tomography, and other structural inference problems. EMPIAR Processing. We take a snapshot of deposited entries within EMPIAR as of June 10, 2026 and apply a series of processing steps. We download particles from the following EMPIAR categories: 1. Picked particles, single frame, processed 2. Picked particles, multiframe, processed 3. Picked particles, single frame, unprocessed 4. Picked particles, multiframe, unprocessed In total 229 entries were downloaded, and repeated particle image were de-duplicated by the stack’s basename and particle index. Metadata is extracted from the MRCS or STAR files. We include images without metadata (i.e., no CTF annotations), but cap the contribution to at most 200,000 particles per entry. Unreadable stacks, invalid image dimensions, and out-of-range particle references were excluded. Images are stored in float32 arrays in their native box sizes. The final dataset contains 51,606,609 from 214 EMPIAR entries. OpenProteinSet Processing. We use the mmCIF files provided in the OpenProteinSet. All obsolete PDB entries are excluded, and protein chains from the first structural model are extracted. We apply the biological assembly specific transforms specified in each mmCIF file, which contains separate metadata describing how to construct each assembly. Each assembly is retained in our dataset. Where assembly metadata was not available, the protein chains were concatenated. Structures with resolutions > 5 5 Å were excluded, as well as assemblies with greater than 10,000 residues after symmetry expansion. Structures with unknown resolution are kept. Finally, the assembly coordinates are centered using the mean position of the atoms. The resulting dataset contains 268,647 assemblies. Pretraining Image Formation Arguments. We use CryoJax for our image formation, specifically version 0.5.6 0.5.6 . We simulate all atoms, using the Peng scattering factors [ Peng et al., 1996 ] .

For ViT-S/B/L, we render on a 640 × 640 640\times 640 grid and crop to 384 × 384 384\times 384 to reduce boundary artifacts from the CTF. The higher-resolution ViT-g Gram-teacher branch is described in Appendix B.3 . We randomly sample Å/pixel values such that the rendered protein spans 35-80% of the image extent. We compute this projected span from the rotated atomic coordinates. We list the parameters for the contrast transfer function in Table 2 . We use additive Gaussian white noise, with target SNRs sampled log-uniformly from [ 0.1 , 0.999 ] [0.1,0.999] . The noise variance is the variance of the noiseless, CTF-applied image within a centered circular mask of radius half the image width, divided by the target SNR. EMber produces dense, semantically meaningful features. We recount the training losses from DINOv2 and DINOv3 here for completeness [ Oquab et al., 2024 , Siméoni et al., 2025 ] : (1) DINO Image-Level Objective [ Caron et al., 2021 ] . Both the teacher class token v t C ​ L ​ S v_{t}^{CLS} and the student class token v s C ​ L ​ S v_{s}^{CLS} are passed through an MLP that outputs a set of prototype scores.

Student scores are normalized using a softmax with temperature 0.1 0.1 to obtain p s p_{s} . We use Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization to turn teacher scores into balanced target distributions. The DINO image-level objective is then: ℒ DINO = − Σ ​ p t ​ log ⁡ p s \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DINO}}=-\Sigma p_{t}\log p_{s} (3) Like the backbone, the student head is optimized using gradient descent, while the teacher head is an EMA of the student head. We compare each student global view with the other teacher global view, excluding same-view pairs, and compare each of the eight student local views with both teacher global views. This gives two global-to-global and sixteen local-to-global pairs per training item. The loss sums over all prototypes, and averages over training items and these eighteen view pairs. (2) Masked Image Modeling Objective [ Zhou et al., 2021 ] . Certain patch tokens are masked when passed to the student network. These patch tokens pass through the iBOT head, which is structured identically to the DINO head and produces normalized prototype scores p s ​ i p_{si} . The corresponding tokens are unmasked when provided to the teacher, whose iBOT head produces p t ​ i p_{ti} . The iBOT masked image modeling objective is ℒ iBOT = − Σ ​ p t ​ i ​ log ⁡ p s ​ i \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{iBOT}}=-\Sigma p_{ti}\log{p_{si}} (4) We match teacher and student targets to the same patch positions within the same global view. For each of the student’s global view images, we average the cross entropy over its masked patches and then average over all global view images in the batch. Finally, images without masked patches contribute nothing to the loss but are included in the denominator for the average. (3) KoLeo Loss [ Sablayrolles et al., 2018 ] . The KoLeo loss term acts as a regularizer which promotes features to uniformly span the feature space.

For feature vectors ( x 1 , … , x n ) (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) , it is defined: ℒ KoLeo = − 1 n ∑ i = 1 n log ( d n , i ) \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KoLeo}}=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(d_{n,i}) (5) where d n , i = min i ≠ j ⁡ ‖ x i − x j ‖ d_{n,i}=\min_{i\neq j}||x_{i}-x_{j}|| , the minimum distance from x i x_{i} to any other feature vector. Feature vectors are L 2 L_{2} normalized before computing the KoLeo loss. (4) Gram Anchoring Loss. We use the Gram anchoring loss from DINOv3 during our ViT-g training run. When using the Gram anchoring, we keep a separate Gram teacher, from an earlier checkpoint, in memory which is used to compute the anchoring loss. We enable this loss at step 187,500 187{,}500 , with a 1,000 1{,}000 -step cosine warmup to weight 2.0 2.0 . The Gram teacher is frozen between updates and is refreshed from the EMA teacher after 197,500 197{,}500 , 207,500 207{,}500 , and 217,500 217{,}500 completed optimizer steps. Adopting the notation from DINOv3, suppose we have P P patch features of dimension d d . Let 𝐗 S \mathbf{X}_{S} , a P × d P\times d matrix, denote the student dense features and 𝐗 G \mathbf{X}_{G} the dense features of the Gram teacher. The Gram anchoring loss is: ℒ Gram = 1 P 2 ​ ∑ i = 1 P ∑ j = 1 P [ ( 𝐗 S ​ 𝐗 S ⊤ ) i ​ j − ( 𝐗 G ​ 𝐗 G ⊤ ) i ​ j ] 2 . \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Gram}}=\frac{1}{P^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{P}\sum_{j=1}^{P}\left[(\mathbf{X}_{S}\mathbf{X}_{S}^{\top})_{ij}-(\mathbf{X}_{G}\mathbf{X}_{G}^{\top})_{ij}\right]^{2}. (6) Each patch-feature vector is L 2 L_{2} normalized before constructing the similarity matrices. We average this loss over global-view images. Combined Loss Function.

Put together, the pretraining loss function is: ℒ = w D ​ ℒ DINO + ℒ iBOT + w K ​ ℒ KoLeo + w G ​ ℒ Gram \displaystyle\mathcal{L}=w_{D}\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}+w_{K}\mathcal{L}_{\text{KoLeo}}+w_{G}\mathcal{L}_{\text{Gram}} (7) We use a DINO loss weight of w D = 1.0 w_{D}=1.0 and KoLeo loss weight of w K = 0.1 w_{K}=0.1 . w G w_{G} is set to 0 when Gram anchoring is disabled and reaches 2.0 2.0 after the warmup when it is enabled. When we use gradient accumulation, each microbatch loss is divided by the number of accumulation steps before backpropagation. Architectures, Optimizer, LR Schedule, Data-Mixing We inherit the architectural choices of DINOv3, and list the architectural hyperparameters of each model size in Table 3 . Hyperparameters for DINOv2 and DINOv3 are from Table 2 by Siméoni et al. [2025] . Target Distributions, Temperatures, and Teacher Momentum. We use a softmax temperature of 0.1 for both student heads. For the DINO teacher, the temperature is held constant at 0.04 for the first 1,250 optimizer steps, then increases linearly from 0.04 to 0.07 until step 30,000, at which point it remains constant for the duration of training. We have a similar schedule for the iBOT teacher. Its temperature increases linearly from 0.04 to 0.07 from steps 0 to 30,000, and then remains constant. For both teacher heads, we exponentiate the scores divided by their respective temperatures and apply three Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations. This normalization helps to balance the prototype mass across all distributed ranks and produces a probability distribution over prototypes for each token. DINO balancing uses all the teacher global view class tokens, while iBOT balancing uses only masked patches in the corresponding student inputs. Unlike some DINO implementations, we do not use running mean-based teacher centering.

We update the teacher parameters using an exponential moving average with momentum 0.994, increased to 0.999 when we start using Gram anchoring. Across all models, we use a global batch size of 3072. Depending on the available compute capacity, we use either no gradient accumulation or 2 steps. For backbone parameters that are exactly two-dimensional tensors, we use Muon [ Jordan et al., 2024 , Liu et al., 2025 ] while remaining backbone parameters use AdamW. Both iBOT and DINO head parameters are updated with AdamW [ Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ] . Muon uses a momentum of 0.95, Nesterov updates, and five Newton-Schulz iterations.

We scale matrix updates by a factor proportional to the layer dimensions so that the update norm aligns with AdamW. For AdamW, we use ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} , with ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) for the backbone and ( 0.9 , 0.99 ) (0.9,0.99) for both projection heads. We use a weight decay of 0.05, excluding biases, normalization parameters, and LayerScale coefficients. This choice follows empirical recommendations to optimize final prediction layers with AdamW when using Muon [ Jordan et al., 2024 ] ; we extend this choice to the complete projection heads for a uniform head optimization scheme. We use a base learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} tuned at a batch size of 256, scaling the learning rate by the square root of the target batch size (3072). All models are trained for 265,000 optimizer steps with gradient clipping set to 3.0. We use a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) [ Wen et al., 2024 ] learning rate scheduler. The global learning rate is linearly warmed up for 15,000 steps, held stable for 223,500 steps, and decayed using 26,500 steps (10% of the total schedule). Patch-embedding parameters use 0.2 times the global learning rate throughout training. We freeze the final prototype projections of both the DINO and iBOT heads for the first 1,250 optimizer steps by setting their learning rates to zero, and linearly increasing to one over the following 13,750 steps, applied multiplicatively to the global learning-rate schedule. When running evaluations, we periodically branch and decay the learning rate over a 10% cooldown period following η ⁡ ( p ) = η peak ​ ( 1 − p ) \eta(p)=\eta_{\mathrm{peak}}(1-\sqrt{p}) , where p ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] p\in[0,1] denotes progress through the decay phase. Data-Mixing Schedule. We find that introducing too much experimental data at the start of training destabilizes training and causes representation collapse. As a result, we use a heuristic schedule which we find to stably train.

During the first 50,000 steps, as part of pre-training, experimental images comprised 6.25% of each batch. We transition to mid-training by increasing the experimental data mix to 50% over the next 50,000 steps using a cosine ramp with a progress exponent of 1.2. From step 100,000 onward, we maintained a mean experimental fraction of 50% and vary the batch composition by using a beta distribution with a dispersion factor of 0.4: f exp ∼ Beta ​ ( 2.625 , 2.625 ) f_{\text{exp}}\sim\text{Beta}(2.625,2.625) . Fig. 9 shows the continuous schedule. In practice, we round the experimental fraction to adjacent multiples of 6.25% to limit the number of batch shapes requiring compilation on each rank in CryoJax. We use different preprocessing for each model, reproducing publicly documented inference pipelines when possible. For EMber , we standardize each image to zero mean and unit variance. For Cryo-IEF, we first apply min–max scaling to each image, and then normalize using the mean and standard deviation in their GitHub repo. For CryoUNI we standardize each image to zero mean and unit variance, CTF phase flip (when known), and use Fourier-resampling if applicable. Model checkpoints. In this evaluation, we use EMPIAR entries 10005, 10017, 10028, 10059, 10061, 10075, 10081, 10093, 10096, 10184, 10240, 10289, 10291, 10345, 10387, 10406, 10444, 10526, 10532, 10576, 10590, 10669, 10671, 10737, 10760, 10816, 11051, 11057, and 11183. Probe methodology.

In this probe, a set of labeled training images are embedded using the model and a final representation is produced by concatenating the [CLS] token and mean pooling the spatial patch features [ Oquab et al., 2024 ] . For EMber , we ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalize each concatenated representation in both the labeled feature bank and the query set. For each query, we select the k k bank particles with highest cosine similarity. We assign each selected neighbor a weight proportional to e s / 0.07 e^{s/0.07} , where s s is the cosine similarity to the query, and normalize these weights over the selected neighbors. We sum the weights by EMPIAR class and rank classes by their total weight to obtain the top-1 and top-5 predictions. Similar to the natural vision case, we use 29 EMPIAR datasets of picked particles from CryoPPP [ Dhakal et al., 2023 ] , a dataset used for particle picking. We sweep over k = 1 , 5 , 10 , 20 k=1,5,10,20 and report the highest top-1 and top-5 accuracy separately. In the case of a tie we choose the smaller k k . We use the same query set for selecting k k and determining accuracy. TRPV1 example. We visualize two entries containing TRPV1, EMPIAR-10005 and EMPIAR-10059, using PCA and UMAP (Fig. 11 ). The entries overlap substantially in PCA and show partial separation in UMAP. These projections do not distinguish molecular differences from acquisition-specific effects. We sampled uniformly without replacement within each of six species (ADH, aldolase, β \beta -amylase, GDH, IgG, and PKM2), and selected 10,000 particles per species for training (60,000 total) and another 10,000 per species from the remaining particles for held-out evaluation (60,000 total). CAHRA images are provided at a native 288 × 288 288\times 288 pixel resolution. However, prior work demonstrates that training at a lower resolution than test-time results in higher overall results [ Touvron et al., 2019 ] . For this reason, and to provide an equal-FLOPs comparison, we use bilinear interpolation to resize images to 384 2 384^{2} , zero-padding images when necessary to make image dimensions divisible by the patch size. We further ensure that the training and validation sets do not overlap. The experimental particles in the challenge dataset are not contained in the pre-training dataset either. Probing Details. When running the evaluation, we sweep over learning rates 3 × 10 − 5 , 1 × 10 − 4 , 3 × 10 − 4 , 1 × 10 − 3 , 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-5},1\times 10^{-4},3\times 10^{-4},1\times 10^{-3},3\times 10^{-3} using AdamW (weight decay = 0.05 =0.05 ), use a batch size of 256, and take the average over three seeds. We train for 100 epochs, using a learning rate warmup of 5 epochs and a cosine decay for 95 epochs, ending at min learning rate 10 % 10\% of the start. When linear probing, we use a single linear layer which takes in the [CLS] token concatenated with mean pooled patch features. The MLP head is structured to be a linear head, LayerNorm, GELU, and a final linear layer. The input is similarly the concatenated [CLS] and mean pooled patch features.

The CNN is a 3x3 convolution, LayerNorm over channels, GELU, global average pooling, and a final linear layer. We use a hidden feature dimension of 128 for the convolutions, while the MLP hidden dimensions are selected to match the parameter count of the CNN head. We report results over 3 seeds. Fine-tuning Details. We use the same 60,000 training images and 60,000 validation images when doing fine-tuning. We add a linear classification head to the backbone. The linear classification head receives the concatenation of the CLS token and mean-pooled spatial tokens. The entire model is then optimized with a cross entropy loss. We train for 20 epochs using AdamW (weight decay = 0.05 =0.05 , β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999 ), and batch size of 1,024. We sweep learning rates of 1 × 10 − 5 , 3 × 10 − 5 , 1 × 10 − 4 , 3 × 10 − 4 , 1 × 10 − 3 1\times 10^{-5},3\times 10^{-5},1\times 10^{-4},3\times 10^{-4},1\times 10^{-3} , using one epoch of linear warmup followed by cosine decay. Hsp90 Finetuning Conformational Heterogeneity Task Description. Hsp90 is a protein with a conformational change described by the opening of its two chains, CMA and CMB, which we discretize. There are, in total, 400 conformational structures. We simulate 200,000 training images across SNR values of 0.1 ​ – ​ 0.01 0.1\text{--}0.01 , sampling different defocus ( 0.5 ​ – ​ 2.0 0.5\text{--}2.0 μ ​ m \mu\mathrm{m} ), b-factors (1, 100 Å 2 \AA^{2} ), and use an amplitude contrast of 0.1 0.1 . The images are simulated at a 256 2 256^{2} box and an A p ​ i ​ x A_{pix} of 1.0 ​ Å 1.0\AA , and center-cropped to 128 2 128^{2} . During simulation, we apply a random translation sampled from [ 0 , 20 ] [0,20] Å. For the final evaluation, we upsample the images from 128 2 128^{2} to 384 2 384^{2} , our final training resolution. We do full fine-tuning given the training dataset and hold the overall optimization arguments the same across models and checkpoints. Structure Filtering. The molecular dynamics trajectories contain 46,789 frames of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, which contain a continuum of open and closed states of the receptor binding domain. This motion can be described with two collective variables (CV), visualized in Fig. 13 (A). To filter and balance the set of structures we use, we bin the CV space using 1 ∘ increments. We keep bins with at least 100 structures, and for bins with more than 100 structures we randomly sample 100 structures from the bin. As a result, there are 4,500 structures for Spike-Up and another 4,500 for Spike-Down, for a total of 9,000 structures. Image formation and Dataset. Images were rendered at 384 2 384^{2} box size with a pixel size of 0.75 Å. Defocus is sampled uniformly from 0.5–-2.0 μ ​ m \mu\mathrm{m} , and B-factor is sampled uniformly from 1–100 Å 2 \AA^{2} . Amplitude contrast is fixed at 0.1. The microscope voltage is simulated at 300kV. The noise model used is Gaussian white noise, added after applying the CTF, and the variance is computed according to the expected SNR and by computing the variance of the CTF-applied image, with a circular mask of radius 192 192 . Noise was applied across the entire image, and images were stored as unnormalized float16 arrays.

The dataset contained 400,000 images: 250,000 training images and three validation pools of 25,000 images each at fixed SNRs of 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001. We additionally have another 100,000 disjoint images used for the Platt calibration. Training SNRs were sampled continuously and uniformly in log space over 0.001–0.1. Optimization Settings. We train a linear classifier on the model features, mapping from the representation to a binary prediction task. We train probes across a range of training images, including 5k, 25k, 50k, and 250k training images. The images are drawn uniformly from the up and down conformations. Similar to the Hsp90 setting, we stratify the validation sets according to SNR: 0.1 , 0.01 0.1,0.01 , and 0.001 0.001 . At each SNR level, we generate 25,000 images per class, evaluating ratios of 0.50 , 0.60 , 0.70 , 0.80 , 0.90 0.50,0.60,0.70,0.80,0.90 and 0.95 0.95 . For evaluation, each fixed-SNR validation pool was divided into 10,000 images for learning-rate selection and 15,000 images for final evaluation, with equal class counts in both partitions. Population estimation used mixtures of 5,000 images sampled without replacement, across 10 sampling seeds. Mixed-SNR evaluation pooled the three final validation partitions into a 45,000-image pool before mixture sampling. We use three different optimizer seeds when running the evaluation, training a new classifier for each seed. This gives us 30 different population estimates per ground truth proportion. We sweep over learning rates 1 ​ e − 4 , 3 ​ e − 4 , 1 ​ e − 3 , 3 ​ e − 3 , 1 ​ e − 2 , 3 ​ e − 2 , 1 ​ e − 1 , 3 ​ e − 1 , 1.0 , 1.5 1e^{-4},3e^{-4},1e^{-3},3e^{-3},1e^{-2},3e^{-2},1e^{-1},3e^{-1},1.0,1.5 for batch size 256 when training the probe, using the held out validation loss to select the optimal learning rate. We train for 100 epochs, using a cosine annealing learning rate scheduler, and batch size 1024 with learning rate scaled according to the square root scaling rule.

The EM algorithm is capped to a max of 50k iterations, and we use a convergence tolerance of 0.01. Synthetic Structure Reconstruction Evaluating Map Reconstructions. Due to the nature of cryo-EM, there are no ground-truth labels for the structures. The canonical method for determining map quality is the resolution derived from the Fourier shell correlation (FSC). The FSC is the normalized cross-correlation between corresponding Fourier shells of two volumes. When evaluating a map against a known reference, the spatial frequency at which the FSC crosses 0.5, corresponding to equal signal and noise, is reported as the resolution. When a reference map is not available, the observed images are split into two half-sets that independently undergo reconstruction. The spatial frequency at which the FSC crosses 0.143 is then reported as the resolution of the resulting map. For a full derivation, refer to Rosenthal and Henderson [2003] . For both Tomotwin-8 and Hsp90, we visualize the FSC curves in Fig. 15 and Fig. 16 . RELION Reconstruction Parameters and Resolution Assignment. For each particle cluster, we reconstruct one volume with the ground truth poses using the relion_reconstruct command in RELION version 4.0.1. Reconstructions used C1 symmetry, CTF correction, and the original full-resolution particle images with ground-truth orientations, translations, and CTF parameters from the source STAR files. Reconstruction pixel sizes were 1.5 Å for Hsp90 and 0.5 Å for TomoTwin. Each reconstruction was compared against every ground-truth reference, and we evaluate resolution at an FSC of 0.5 since we have a reference structure and do not use half-maps. Because we a priori do not know which cluster belongs to which structure, we exhaustively search for pairings which produce the lowest mean resolution. Latent k k -Means clustering. Clustering used scikit-learn’s KMeans with k-means++ initialization, 10 initializations, and a fixed random seed of 0.

The solution with the lowest within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances was retained. We use a convergence tolerance of 1 ​ e − 4 1e^{-4} , and always set k k to the number of ground truth structures. CryoDRGN-AI settings. We use cryoDRGN-AI 4.3.0 and a latent dimension of eight. The decoder output and loss are on Fourier downsampled 128 2 128^{2} images, but the encoders are always provided full resolution images. This is done to make the cryoDRGN-AI training computationally tractable. 10,000 images are used to initialize the decoder with random poses, followed by three epochs of hierarchical pose search. Pose search retained eight candidate poses per image and used four refinement iterations. The translation-search grid used seven points per axis, and an extent parameter of 20 pixels. We use Adam with a learning rate of 1 ​ e − 4 1e^{-4} for the reconstruction network and encoder head, and 1 ​ e − 2 1e^{-2} for the conformation table when applicable. These values were chosen from the recommended defaults. Batch size was set to 16. The decoder network uses a width of 256, three layers, and Gaussian positional encoding with dimension 64 and feature scale 0.5 in the Hartley domain. Probe Head Structures. We use a dense spatial head on the two-dimensional grid of ViT patch tokens. It comprised a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution followed by three 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolutions with stride two, with output channel widths of 256, 384, 512, and 512. Each layer uses group norm with 32 groups, GELU activations, and a final tanh activation. This is then projected down to an eight-dimensional latent space. Hsp90 Details Image Generation. Orientations are sampled uniformly over SO(3), and translations were sampled uniformly from -10 to +10 Å. Mean defocus, astigmatism magnitude, and astigmatism angle were sampled uniformly over 10,000–15,000 Å, 0–100 Å, and 0–180 ∘ , respectively.
